# The provenance file on Skr

*Provenance record 494 · Skr · one temple, fully accounted for.*

## Provenance

**1. The attestation.** **𓋴𓎡𓂋𓅃**, from the tradition's own record. On record: Memphite funerary liturgies and the Shabaka Stone tradition, Sokar-festival reliefs and Henu-barque iconography, Deir el-Medina ostraca (craft invocations), Griffiths, ‘Sokar’ in Lexikon der Ägyptologie.

**2. The narrative record.** **The Mound in the Necropolis** — Sokar’s domain was not merely burial-ground but cosmogram: the Memphite desert’s hillocks were read as the world’s first mound rising from Nun.  His priests raised the Djed-pillar there each year — Osiris’ backbone set upright in Sokar’s earth — and the world’s order was reaffirmed at the threshold of the dead. **The Voyage of the Funerary Falcon** — The Sokar-festival’s climax was the procession of the Henu: a ship-shaped shrine on a sledge, its prow a falcon-head, drawn around the Memphite walls at dawn.  The dead of the necropolis were imagined sailing with him; the barque’s circuit through the desert gates was the afterlife’s rehearsal.

**3. The physical record.** His Memphite shrines are largely lost beneath the cultivation, but the Henu-barque amulets by the thousand, the Djed-pillar iconography, and the Saqqara Serapeum’s older strata preserve his cult’s materiality. The Late Period shaft-tombs of the sacred animals at Saqqara ran through ground his priests had held for millennia.

**4. The current holding.** The temple at [/sokar/](/sokar/), a temple of the restored name. aSCII-equivalent form

**5. The documented resonances.** **Funerary & Memorial Services**, **Manufacturing, Craft & Automation**, **Architecture & Spatial Design** — seats argued and weighted in the [pattern atlas](/patterns/), read through the myths in this temple's [Resonance File](/sokar/blog/resonance/).

**6. The primary sources.** [The Book of the Dead](/texts/book-of-the-dead/) — the library this file answers to, open at the [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/).

**7. The continuing record.** His festival ship, the Henu, survives in hundreds of amulets and in the standard late coffin-foot vignette; and the Djed-raising rite he hosted became the emblematic ‘erection of Osiris’ celebrated at the New Year across Egypt.  The Memphite trinity remains the textbook example of Egyptian god-compounding done to completion.
